blocks.text: A 25-year-old woman has had eight watery, bloody stools a day for ten days, with urgency and a night-time need to pass stool. Her sister, with a different disease, has had pale, bulky, floating stools and iron-deficiency anaemia for years. Both have bowel inflammation or damage that interferes with how the gut works; the pattern of symptoms, the colonoscopy and a few well-chosen tests sort them out.

blocks.markdown: The small intestine digests and absorbs nutrients through villi and microvilli; the colon absorbs water and electrolytes and stores faeces. **Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)** is chronic, relapsing immune-mediated inflammation of the gut, arising in genetically susceptible people from an abnormal immune response to gut bacteria. The two main forms are **Crohn disease** and **ulcerative colitis (UC)**. **Malabsorption** is failure to absorb nutrients and may be caused by small bowel disease (coeliac disease, Crohn disease), pancreatic insufficiency or bile acid and bacterial problems. **Coeliac disease** is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten in genetically susceptible (HLA-DQ2 or DQ8) individuals.

rows: Anywhere from mouth to anus; terminal ileum and colon most often; skip lesions
Rectum always involved, extends proximally and continuously
Non-caseating granulomas, deep fissuring ulcers, cobblestone appearance
Crypt abscesses, goblet cell depletion, diffuse mucosal inflammation
Abdominal pain, diarrhoea (often non-bloody), weight loss, perianal disease
Toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, primary sclerosing cholangitis
blocks.caption: Crohn disease versus ulcerative colitis.

blocks.markdown: **Investigation of IBD.** Blood tests show anaemia, raised CRP and platelets, and low albumin. **Faecal calprotectin**, a neutrophil protein in stool, distinguishes IBD from irritable bowel syndrome in patients with diarrhoea. Stool cultures and *Clostridioides difficile* toxin exclude infection. Colonoscopy with ileal intubation and biopsies makes the diagnosis; MRI or capsule imaging assesses the small bowel in Crohn disease. In acute severe UC the Truelove and Witts criteria define severity: six or more bloody stools a day plus at least one sign of systemic upset (pulse above 90 per minute, temperature above 37.8 degrees C, haemoglobin below 105 g/L, ESR above 30 mm/h).

blocks.caption: Percentage weight loss, a simple malnutrition marker (loss above 10% over 3 to 6 months is clinically significant).

blocks.title: How much weight has been lost?
blocks.prompt: A patient with small bowel Crohn disease weighed 70 kg six months ago and now weighs 62 kg. Calculate the percentage weight loss and say whether it is clinically significant.

steps.text: Express as a percentage of usual weight.
Over 10% in about 6 months is significant, so assess nutrition (dietitian input, vitamin and iron status) and consider enteral nutrition alongside treating the inflammation.

blocks.markdown: **Diagnosing coeliac disease and other malabsorption.** In coeliac disease, gluten peptides provoke a T-cell response that causes villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis in the duodenum. Presentations include diarrhoea, bloating, weight loss, iron, B12 or folate deficiency, osteoporosis, dermatitis herpetiformis and an association with type 1 diabetes. **Serum IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody (tTG)** is the first test, with total IgA measured because IgA deficiency gives false negatives, and it only works if the patient is **still eating gluten** (several slices of bread daily for at least 6 weeks). In adults, positive serology is followed by duodenal biopsies at endoscopy to confirm villous atrophy. Treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet. Other tests: faecal elastase for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, breath tests for small bowel bacterial overgrowth, and quantitative faecal fat in selected cases.

blocks.caption: In health, over 93% of dietary fat is absorbed (a figure that varies with method).

blocks.title: Quantifying steatorrhoea
blocks.prompt: A patient eats 100 g of fat per day on a measured diet and excretes 12 g in stool per day. Calculate the fat absorption coefficient.

steps.text: Fat absorbed is intake minus faecal loss: 100 - 12 = 88 g/day.
88% is below the normal value of over 93%, indicating fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea). Faecal elastase and duodenal biopsy would help locate the cause.

items: Ulcerative colitis, induction of remission: mild to moderate disease is treated with aminosalicylates (mesalazine, topical rectal and/or oral); if there is no response add oral prednisolone. Acute severe colitis needs admission, IV hydrocortisone, thromboprophylaxis and early surgical review; rescue therapy is infliximab or ciclosporin.
UC maintenance: aminosalicylate for most patients; azathioprine or biologics for frequent relapse. Colectomy is curative for the bowel disease.
Crohn disease, induction: corticosteroids (or exclusive enteral nutrition in children); add anti-TNF biologics for severe or refractory disease. Stop smoking.

Crohn maintenance: azathioprine, mercaptopurine or methotrexate, or a biologic. Aminosalicylates are not effective for maintaining remission in Crohn disease. Surgery is for strictures, fistulae and failure of medical therapy but is not curative.
General: monitor bone health, iron, B12 and folate; screen for colorectal cancer after long-standing colitis.

blocks.title: Induce then maintain
blocks.text: IBD therapy has two phases: a rapid induction of remission, usually corticosteroids or biologics, and long-term maintenance with a steroid-sparing agent. Steroids are not used for maintenance because of their adverse effects.

points: Crohn disease is patchy and transmural with granulomas and may affect any gut segment; UC is continuous from the rectum and confined to the mucosa.
Faecal calprotectin and colonoscopy with biopsy diagnose IBD; tTG-IgA on a gluten-containing diet is the first test for coeliac disease, confirmed by duodenal biopsy in adults.
Induction uses aminosalicylates, steroids or biologics; maintenance uses aminosalicylates in UC, and thiopurines, methotrexate or biologics in Crohn disease.
Quantify malnutrition and steatorrhoea with percentage weight loss and fat absorption.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old smoker has right iliac fossa pain, weight loss, non-bloody diarrhoea and a perianal fistula. Colonoscopy shows patchy ulceration with normal intervening mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: skip lesions, perianal disease, smoking and weight loss.
distractorRationale.b: UC is continuous from the rectum with bloody diarrhoea.
distractorRationale.c: Coeliac disease affects the duodenum and does not cause perianal fistulae.
distractorRationale.d: IBS does not cause mucosal ulceration or fistulae.

questions.explanation: Skip lesions and perianal fistulae are characteristic of Crohn disease, which is transmural and can affect any part of the gut. Smoking worsens Crohn disease.

questions.stem: Which histological finding is most characteristic of Crohn disease rather than ulcerative colitis?

options.text: Crypt abscesses confined to the mucosa
Continuous inflammation starting at the rectum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Crohn disease is transmural and may show granulomas.
distractorRationale.b: Crypt abscesses confined to mucosa are typical of UC.
distractorRationale.c: Villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytes is coeliac disease.
distractorRationale.d: Continuous rectal-onset inflammation describes UC, though it is not a histological finding.

questions.explanation: Crohn disease inflames the full thickness of the bowel wall and may form non-caseating granulomas, which explains fistulae and strictures. UC is limited to the mucosa and submucosa with crypt abscesses.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has iron-deficiency anaemia, bloating and loose stools. She eats bread and pasta daily. What is the most appropriate first test for coeliac disease?

options.text: Serum IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA

questions.correctOptionText: Serum IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA

distractorRationale.a: Correct: first-line serology while on gluten.
distractorRationale.c: The urea breath test detects H. pylori.
distractorRationale.d: Calprotectin detects intestinal inflammation as in IBD.

questions.explanation: Serum tTG-IgA is the first test and is accurate only while the patient is eating gluten. Total IgA is measured to exclude IgA deficiency, which would cause false negatives, and positive serology is then confirmed by duodenal biopsy in adults.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis has weight loss and pale, bulky stools that are hard to flush. Which test best confirms the cause of his malabsorption?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: low faecal elastase indicates pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
distractorRationale.b: tTG-IgA tests for coeliac disease, which is not suggested.
distractorRationale.c: Colonoscopy would not assess pancreatic enzyme output.
distractorRationale.d: Anti-smooth muscle antibody relates to autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.explanation: Steatorrhoea after chronic pancreatitis results from lipase deficiency, which faecal elastase detects. Treatment is pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with known ulcerative colitis is admitted with 9 bloody stools a day, pulse 112 per minute, temperature 38.1 degrees C and CRP 95 mg/L. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone with thromboprophylaxis and early surgical review

questions.correctOptionText: Intravenous hydrocortisone with thromboprophylaxis and early surgical review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acute severe colitis is treated with IV corticosteroids and close monitoring.
distractorRationale.b: Oral mesalazine alone is insufficient for severe disease.
distractorRationale.d: Azathioprine is a maintenance agent that acts too slowly.

questions.explanation: Six or more bloody stools a day with tachycardia and fever meets the Truelove and Witts criteria for acute severe colitis. Intravenous steroid induces remission in many, and rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin, or colectomy, is considered if there is no response after about three days.

questions.stem: A patient with Crohn disease weighed 84 kg six months ago and now weighs 75 kg. Calculate the percentage weight loss.
questions.explanation: Percentage loss = (84 - 75) / 84 x 100 = 10.7%. Loss above 10% over 3 to 6 months is clinically significant and prompts nutritional assessment.

questions.stem: On a controlled diet containing 90 g of fat per day, a patient excretes 18 g of fat in stool per day. Calculate the fat absorption coefficient as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Absorbed fat is 90 - 18 = 72 g, and 72 / 90 x 100 = 80%. This is well below the normal value of over 93%, confirming steatorrhoea.

questions.stem: Contrast the clinical and pathological features of Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
markingGuide: Distribution: Crohn any part of gut with skip lesions; UC rectum and continuous proximal extension
Depth: Crohn transmural; UC mucosal and submucosal
Histology: Crohn non-caseating granulomas; UC crypt abscesses
Symptoms: Crohn pain, weight loss, non-bloody diarrhoea, perianal disease; UC bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus
Complications: Crohn strictures, fistulae; UC toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer, PSC
Smoking: worsens Crohn, protective in UC
questions.explanation: The depth and distribution of inflammation explain the symptoms. Transmural disease leads to fistulae and strictures in Crohn disease, while mucosal inflammation in UC causes bleeding and urgency.

questions.stem: Outline the principles of induction and maintenance therapy in Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
markingGuide: Two phases: induce remission then maintain it
UC mild to moderate: aminosalicylate (topical and/or oral), then oral steroid if no response
UC severe: admission, IV hydrocortisone, rescue with infliximab or ciclosporin, or colectomy
UC maintenance: aminosalicylate, azathioprine or biologic
Crohn induction: corticosteroids (or enteral nutrition in children); biologics for severe disease
Crohn maintenance: azathioprine, mercaptopurine, methotrexate or biologic; aminosalicylates not effective
Steroids not used for maintenance; surgery in specific situations
questions.explanation: Steroids induce remission quickly but cannot be used long-term because of adverse effects, so steroid-sparing drugs maintain it. UC is curable by colectomy, whereas Crohn disease recurs after surgery.

questions.stem: True or false: serum tTG-IgA remains a reliable screening test for coeliac disease in a patient who has followed a strict gluten-free diet for the past 6 months.
questions.explanation: The antibody response depends on continued gluten exposure, so serology and biopsies can be falsely negative after gluten withdrawal. The patient should resume gluten for at least 6 weeks before testing.
